packSfmcToMcn.postureStatement: Before you start, one thing about how we will read your answers. We can read your current Marketing Cloud estate directly, so the journey, data extension and automation figures in your readout are measured rather than described. Nothing writes to Marketing Cloud Next yet, so the target-side model is the accelerator's working picture of the platform and several entries are pending verification against a real tenant.

gates.readoutBlock: MCN Consent & Custom Preferences is a Spring '26+ capability and its parity with what you run today is unverified. With permission state this entangled, the preference-centre rebuild must not sit on the critical path: bridge it on the current platform and rebuild after parity is confirmed against a real tenant. Plan 2-4 weeks for a custom consent model on top of the foundation estimate.

Marketing Cloud Next runs on Data Cloud. With no Data 360 footprint in place, the Foundation phase gates every other lane — journey, content and campaign work cannot complete before the data layer exists. Budget 8-16 weeks of foundation before migration build starts, plus 4 weeks if Identity Resolution is not yet configured. This does not change the readiness score: the estate may well be easy to move, and still not be movable yet.

The named target sits on Salesforce Core, and there is no Salesforce footprint to sit it on. A platform-precursor project — org, licences, user model, governance — has to land before any marketing migration can be scheduled, and it is a different budget line with a different sponsor. Raise it now rather than at contracting: it is the single most common reason an otherwise-ready migration slips a quarter.

callouts.workaround: Track flow entry in a DMO and use it as a segment exclusion.
callouts.issue: Source orchestration relies on re-entry rules or entry suppression
callouts.gloss: Campaign Flow has no 'No Re-entry' equivalent yet

callouts.workaround: Generate a Calculated Insight per required engagement signal and reference it in the Decision element.
callouts.issue: Source branches on email open/click behaviour
callouts.gloss: There is no Engagement Split element; engagement is a Calculated Insight read by a Decision element

callouts.workaround: Pre-calculate segment-membership boolean as a Calculated Insight.
callouts.issue: Source evaluates segment/filter membership at runtime
callouts.gloss: Segment membership is evaluable via Calculated Insight, not at Flow runtime directly

callouts.workaround: Confirm platform event configuration and wait granularity in the tenant before relying on either.
callouts.issue: Source relies on precise wait timing or event-based pauses
callouts.gloss: Wait element semantics and event-based pause behaviour are working assumptions in the accelerator's model

callouts.workaround: Start SMS re-provisioning immediately and in parallel; do not wait for the Foundation phase.
callouts.issue: SMS, push or short-code sending is in scope
callouts.gloss: Senders and short codes are re-provisioned, never transferred, and this is the longest lead time in the programme

callouts.workaround: Three resolution paths, in preference order: a single-attribute read becomes a merge field; a lookup or calculation becomes a Calculated Insight referenced in the template; a recommendation becomes an Einstein Personalization slot. Each gap needs human review.
manualSteps: Inventory AMPscript constructs in source email
Classify each as merge-field / CI / Einstein
Rebuild the email asset in Content Studio with the chosen primitive
Validate rendered output against samples
callouts.issue: Email asset contains AMPscript that has no direct SFMC Next equivalent
callouts.gloss: AMPscript does not exist in SFMC Next

callouts.workaround: Re-model the DE as a DMO. The accelerator emits a DMO contract (schema only); the operator wires Data Cloud ingestion.
manualSteps: Review emitted dmo_<name>.json
Create DMO in Data Cloud workspace
Configure DLO + ingestion stream OR mapping from existing DMO
Run Identity Resolution if the DMO joins on Individual
callouts.issue: Journey reads from or writes to a Data Extension (no DE concept in SFMC Next)
callouts.gloss: DEs are replaced by DMOs in Data Cloud

callouts.workaround: Reject the source journey; the operator configures Activation Limits in the tenant.
manualSteps: Mark source journey as rejected in IR
Configure Activation Limits per channel in Marketing Cloud Growth Setup
Document weekly/monthly cap policy in tenant runbook
callouts.issue: Source journey is a frequency-capping proxy (DE-driven cap logic)
callouts.gloss: SFMC Next has native channel-level Activation Limits

callouts.workaround: Rearchitect each query as a Data 360 transform or Calculated Insight; complex SQL is a redesign, not a port.
callouts.issue: Audience preparation depends on Automation Studio SQL
callouts.gloss: Batch SQL is largely replaced by declarative transforms, Calculated Insights and Flow

supplements.question: What does the destination tenant look like today — is there an MCE instance, does it have a business-unit structure, and is it agreed which brand or region lands in which BU?

options.label: No MCE tenant provisioned, or one exists that nobody administers. Business-unit structure is undecided.
A tenant and some business units exist, but which brand, region or source instance lands where has not been agreed.
Tenant and business units are live and administered, and every brand or region has an agreed destination BU.

supplements.question: In Marketing Cloud, is there an agreed subscriber key and a modelled set of sendable data extensions — or would the audience model be designed from scratch as part of this migration?

options.label: Nothing modelled. No agreed subscriber key, no sendable data extensions, no attribute sets.
Some sendable DEs exist for tactical sends, built ad hoc. No agreed subscriber key and no attribute-set design.
A subscriber key is agreed, sendable DEs and attribute sets are modelled, and Contact Builder is the audience source of truth.

supplements.question: Is there a send-frequency policy, and does the suppression infrastructure that enforces it exist in the target tenant yet?

options.label: No policy and no infrastructure. How often a contact is mailed is whatever the campaign calendar produces.
A cap policy exists — in the current platform's settings or on paper — but nothing is built target-side to enforce it.
The suppression data extension and its automation are in place target-side, and the cap windows are agreed.

supplements.question: Looking past this migration: is there anything you are hoping to get from the wider Salesforce stack later — Marketing Cloud Next capabilities, or Data 360 / Data Cloud as the eventual home for your data model — rather than from Marketing Cloud Engagement itself? Does Sales own HubSpot Sequences, and does anyone consider them in scope for this migration?
When marketing reporting changes shape, who signs it off?

slots.respondentHint: Useful to have to hand: your counts of active workflows, lists, marketing emails published in the last 12 months, live landing pages and live forms, and the number of portals you run.

options.label: 500+ active campaigns or programs, or six or more business units / separate instances
150-500 active campaigns or programs, or three to five business units

slots.respondentHint: Worth checking before you answer: who holds HubSpot Super Admin, whether your security team allows private apps at all, and who would create the Marketing Cloud installed package. That last one is often a different team.

options.label: No HubSpot admin access, no owner, nobody has exported anything before — and no Marketing Cloud tenant or credentials to write to.

options.label: A supported connector reads the source directly with no operator in the loop.

slots.ceilingReason: No HubSpot connector ships today. The best available path is an operator-run extract against a scoped private app, which is what a 3 describes — so a 4 is not on offer for this pair, for anyone. slots.respondentHint: If you are not sure, open one of your busier workflows: 're-enrol contacts' and 'goal' are checkboxes in its settings, and a go-to-action step is visible on the canvas.

slots.respondentHint: Useful to have to hand: how many email templates you have used in the last 12 months, which custom modules appear in those emails, and how many of the templates exist in more than one language.
slots.question: Thinking only about your marketing emails, which would be rebuilt as Content Builder templates and assets: how many email templates are in real use, how much of each is custom modules and HubL doing real logic rather than standard modules and copy, and how many language variants are maintained? Some custom modules and conditional HubL in emails, but the logic is over the contact's own properties and rewrites cleanly into AMPscript and a Data Extension lookup.
Templates and copy only, few enough to rebuild deliberately, with personalisation that is merge fields and nothing more.

slots.measures: Template governance versus bespoke code and scripting depth
slots.label: Email Content Portability
slots.evidencePrompt: Ask for two counts and one ratio: email templates used in the last 12 months, modules ranked by usage IN EMAILS (not across the site), and how many of those templates exist in more than one language. The estimate is per construct and per template, not per email. Do NOT count landing pages, site pages or blog templates here — whether any of that is even moving is the cms_scope_expectation probe, not this slot.

slots.respondentHint: Two things worth knowing before you answer: who logs into HubSpot who is not in marketing and what they do there, and whether you could name the single field that would identify a subscriber in the new platform.
slots.question: In HubSpot, the CRM and the marketing platform are the same product. How much of your customer data model would have to move with the marketing estate, who else is using it, and does the part marketing needs decompose into a subscriber and a set of sendable tables?

options.label: HubSpot IS the CRM. Sales works in it daily, deals and pipeline live there, and nobody can say which properties marketing actually sends on.
HubSpot CRM is in real use by at least one non-marketing team, and custom objects, associations or shared properties are read by marketing automation.
Marketing's audience needs are known and mostly contact-level: a subscriber key is identifiable and the rest would land as a handful of sendable tables.
The system of record for the customer is already elsewhere and in scope; HubSpot holds marketing attributes that decompose cleanly into a subscriber plus sendable data extensions.

slots.measures: Schema documentation and audience reuse versus per-campaign silos
slots.label: CRM & Data Model Entanglement
slots.evidencePrompt: Ask who logs into HubSpot who is not in marketing, and what they do there. Then ask what would be the subscriber key — if the answer is a discussion rather than a field name, this is not a 3.

slots.respondentHint: Worth knowing before you answer: which teams own the integrations connected to HubSpot, and whether any of your forms or CTAs are embedded on pages another team looks after.
slots.question: Of the things wired into HubSpot — app-marketplace integrations, forms and CTAs embedded on sites you do not control, webhooks, Operations Hub custom code, ad-audience syncs — how many are owned by a team outside marketing, and how many would have to be re-pointed by someone else before you could switch off HubSpot?

options.label: Several are owned outside marketing, including forms or CTAs embedded on sites another team controls, and nobody has a full list of who owns what.
The main ones are known and at least one sits with another team, so cutover depends on a schedule marketing does not set.
A small number of integrations, all with a named owner inside or beside marketing, and any embedded forms are on pages we control.
Nothing outside marketing depends on HubSpot. Forms are on our own pages and the integrations we have could be re-pointed by this team alone.

slots.measures: External forms and integrations posting into the platform
slots.label: Integration Containment
slots.evidencePrompt: Ask for the installed-apps list, the connected ad accounts, and the count of forms embedded outside their own domain. The last one is the number they will not have. Then ask, per item, who would have to do the work — the answer that matters is the owner, not the count, which Integration Surface already collects.

slots.respondentHint: Useful to have to hand: whether your subscription records show when and how consent was given, and whether anything outside HubSpot also holds that state.
slots.question: Where does subscription and consent state live — HubSpot subscription types with a lawful basis, the account-level suppression layer, or somewhere outside the platform entirely — and how many distinct subscription types are in use?

options.label: Consent is subscription types plus list membership, with no record of when or how it was given, and nobody is sure how many types are live.
Subscription types are used properly and lawful basis is recorded, but only inside HubSpot, and there are more types than a publication-list model would absorb without collapsing some together.
Subscription state has provenance and a small enough type set to map one-to-one onto publication lists, or is mirrored outside HubSpot and could be re-established.
A system in scope already masters consent as cross-channel policy, verified against current sending behaviour, and Marketing Cloud would consume it rather than own it.

slots.label: Consent & Preference Portability
slots.evidencePrompt: Ask for the count of subscription types and the count of publication lists the target would have. Where the first number is bigger than the second, ask which types would be merged — that merge is the compliance risk, and it is a decision someone has to sign.

slots.question: Who decides what moves, what is retired and what is rebuilt — and who validates it afterwards?

options.label: No named owner for those decisions, and nobody free to validate the result
An owner exists in principle but has little time; validation would fall to one already-busy person
A named owner per area, with some capacity set aside to review and test
A named decision owner and named validators, with time formally allocated to the migration

slots.measures: Whether humans exist to make disposition decisions and to validate the result
slots.label: Decision Ownership & Validation Capacity

packHubToSfmc.postureStatement: Before you start, one thing about how we will read your answers. The two ends of this move are not equally known. Nothing reads HubSpot — there is no source connector, so every count you give us is your description of the estate rather than a measurement of it. The destination is the opposite: Marketing Cloud Engagement has a real capability manifest, a target adapter that scaffolds against it, and live tenant access. So we treat the estate figures as illustrative and the named gaps as not: they are structural properties of Journey Builder, Content Builder and Data Extensions, and they will be true of your estate whatever its size turns out to be.

gates.readoutBlock: MCN Consent & Custom Preferences is a Spring '26+ capability and its parity with what you run today is unverified. With permission state this entangled, the preference-centre rebuild must not sit on the critical path: bridge it on the current platform and rebuild after parity is confirmed against a real tenant. Plan 2-4 weeks for a custom consent model on top of the foundation estimate.

Marketing Cloud Next runs on Data Cloud. With no Data 360 footprint in place, the Foundation phase gates every other lane — journey, content and campaign work cannot complete before the data layer exists. Budget 8-16 weeks of foundation before migration build starts, plus 4 weeks if Identity Resolution is not yet configured. This does not change the readiness score: the estate may well be easy to move, and still not be movable yet.

The named target sits on Salesforce Core, and there is no Salesforce footprint to sit it on. A platform-precursor project — org, licences, user model, governance — has to land before any marketing migration can be scheduled, and it is a different budget line with a different sponsor. Raise it now rather than at contracting: it is the single most common reason an otherwise-ready migration slips a quarter.

complexityDimensions.respondentHint: Your workflows list shows the active count directly, and each workflow's enrolment trigger is on its first step.
complexityDimensions.question: Roughly how many workflows are switched on in HubSpot right now, and how many of those start from something happening rather than from a schedule?

options.label: Fewer than 20 active workflows, mostly list-based or scheduled enrolment.
Between 20 and 80 active workflows, a mix of list-based enrolment and event or form triggers.
More than 80 active workflows, with enrolment driven mostly by events, webhooks or API calls.

complexityDimensions.respondentHint: Settings then Properties gives you the count per object, and Data Model lists any custom objects.
complexityDimensions.question: How much customer data sits behind your sends — roughly how many contact properties are in use, and do you have custom objects as well as contacts and companies?

options.label: Contacts and companies with mostly HubSpot-standard properties; a few dozen custom properties at most, and no custom objects.
A few hundred custom properties in use, deals or tickets read by marketing, and perhaps one or two custom objects.
Custom properties in the high hundreds or more, several custom objects with their own associations, and calculated or rollup properties feeding segmentation.

complexityDimensions.measures: How much audience data there is, and how many pieces it is in

complexityDimensions.respondentHint: Design Manager lists your custom modules, and custom code and webhook actions appear as steps inside workflows.

complexityDimensions.measures: How much hand-written code is embedded in the estate

complexityDimensions.respondentHint: Business units are an Enterprise feature, so if you have never seen the setting, the answer is almost certainly one portal.

options.label: One portal, with no business units.

Six or more portals or business units, or brands that share content and audiences across several of them.

complexityDimensions.respondentHint: Your installed-apps list and connected ad accounts are both under Settings then Integrations.
complexityDimensions.question: How many other systems are connected to HubSpot — marketplace apps, connected ad accounts, and anything built against the API?

options.label: A CRM or ad-account connection or two from the marketplace, and nothing custom.
Several marketplace apps plus one or two things built against the HubSpot API, and some connected ad accounts.
Many connected apps and ad accounts, plus custom integrations built against the API, and forms embedded on sites beyond our own.

complexityDimensions.measures: How many other systems are wired in
complexityDimensions.label: Connected Systems

complexityDimensions.respondentHint: Your subscription types are listed under Marketing then Email then Subscription Types, with a count at the top.
complexityDimensions.question: How many subscription types are in use, and how many places hold opt-out or suppression state — HubSpot alone, or other systems as well?

options.label: A handful of subscription types, and HubSpot's own opt-out and suppression state is the only record.
Ten or more subscription types, or a preference page we have customised, or one other system that also holds opt-outs.
Dozens of subscription types, per-language or per-brand preference pages, and opt-out state held in more than one other system as well.

complexityDimensions.measures: How many permission categories exist, and how many places they live
complexityDimensions.label: Permission Model Size

callouts.workaround: Convert each active list to a scheduled-refresh audience and set the refresh cadence from the automation's real sensitivity rather than from a default. Where membership is read inside a decision, pre-calculate it as a boolean on the entry Data Extension. Where automatic REMOVAL is load-bearing — suppression lists above all — implement the removal explicitly: a stale suppression list mails people who opted out.
manualSteps: Inventory active lists and the workflows that consume them
For each, establish how fast membership changes must propagate — in minutes, hours or days
Set a refresh cadence per audience from that answer, and write it down as a commitment
Add a boolean per list to the entry DE where a decision reads membership, populated by a Query Activity before entry
Identify every list whose REMOVAL behaviour matters and implement removal explicitly
Audit suppression-role lists first — those are the compliance-relevant ones
callouts.issue: Automation depends on active (smart) list membership that is continuously re-evaluated, including automatic removal
callouts.gloss: HubSpot active lists are live — contacts join AND LEAVE as criteria stop matching. Marketing Cloud cannot evaluate filter membership at runtime, so an active list becomes a scheduled Automation Studio query and membership is stale between runs.

callouts.workaround: This is a scoping decision, not a technical workaround. Three outcomes, with completely different cost and cutover risk: HubSpot stays as the CRM and Marketing Cloud integrates to it via Marketing Cloud Connect; the CRM moves to Sales Cloud; or the estate splits, marketing on Salesforce and sales still in HubSpot. Force it to the surface in Assess and get it decided before Blueprint.
manualSteps: Inventory which CRM objects marketing automation actually reads and writes
Establish whether Sales and Service will remain on HubSpot post-migration
Decide: HubSpot stays as CRM / CRM moves to Sales Cloud / the estate splits
If HubSpot stays, design the integration and name its owner and its budget
If the CRM moves, add a CRM migration workstream — it is not in the marketing scope
callouts.issue: Marketing automation reads and writes CRM records that live in HubSpot's own CRM, not in an external system of record
callouts.gloss: In an Eloqua or SFMC estate the CRM is somewhere else and the marketing platform syncs to it. In HubSpot the CRM IS the platform, so a marketing migration has to answer a question that never arises otherwise: where does the CRM go?

callouts.workaround: Classify each backward edge, then convert it. Poll-until-true becomes Wait By Attribute on a pre-calculated datetime. Retry-N-times becomes an unrolled fixed-count sequence, and the truncation gets documented. Hold-until-eligible is not a loop at all — it routes to the frequency- capping infrastructure. Where nothing fits, split into multiple journeys chained by Fire Event.
manualSteps: Trace every go-to-action edge and mark the ones that point backwards
Classify each backward edge: poll / retry / hold
For poll: pre-calculate the exit datetime or boolean into the entry DE
For retry: unroll to a fixed maximum count and document the truncation
For hold: route to the frequency-capping suppression DE instead
Where nothing else fits, split into multiple journeys connected by Fire Event
callouts.issue: Source workflow uses a go-to-action step that jumps backwards, forming a loop
callouts.gloss: Journey Builder is strictly forward-only — contacts never move backwards. Typical HubSpot loops are poll-until-qualified, retry-N-times and hold-until-eligible.

callouts.workaround: Enable re-entry on the target journey, then build a scheduled Automation Studio query that injects re-qualifying contacts, plus a last-entered-date attribute the injection guards against so nobody enters twice inside the intended window. Validate the cadence against the source's REAL re-enrolment frequency, not against its configuration.
manualSteps: Record each workflow's re-enrolment triggers and its observed re-enrolment frequency
Enable re-entry on the target journey
Build a scheduled Automation Studio query that injects re-qualifiers
Add a last-entered-date attribute and guard the injection against it
Validate re-entry cadence against the source's real behaviour
callouts.issue: Source workflow has re-enrolment enabled — records re-enter on repeat trigger matches
callouts.gloss: Journey Builder has no re-enrolment concept. Entry is per-injection, so the source of repeated entry is rebuilt outside the journey as a scheduled query.

callouts.workaround: Split the goal in two. The exit half becomes journey Exit Criteria, and its evaluation frequency has to be confirmed rather than assumed — HubSpot's is near-continuous. The metric half is a reporting requirement handed to whoever owns reporting; it does not travel with the journey. Flag any workflow whose goal is its only success measure, because that report otherwise disappears silently.
manualSteps: Extract the goal filter for every workflow that has one
Implement the exit half as journey Exit Criteria
Confirm the target's evaluation frequency against HubSpot's near-continuous one
Hand the conversion-metric definition to the reporting workstream explicitly
Flag any workflow whose goal is its ONLY success measure
callouts.issue: Source workflow declares goal criteria that both auto-unenrol records and define the conversion metric
callouts.gloss: A HubSpot goal does two jobs — it exits the record on conversion and it supplies the workflow's headline conversion rate. Journey Builder provides the first as Exit Criteria and the second not at all.

callouts.workaround: Settle the scope question first — read the cms_scope_expectation answer before pricing any of this. If HubSpot CMS is being kept, record the boundary, confirm nothing in the EMAIL estate queries HubDB, and stop here. If the content is expected to move, or an email does query a table, split it into a data problem and a rendering problem. Each HubDB table becomes a Data Extension. Each render-time query becomes either an AMPscript Lookup, for a static lookup, or a value pre-computed into the send audience where it is dynamic per recipient. Listing-style content — a variable-length list rendered from a table — is the case that does not convert; rebuild it as a dynamic block or accept reduced fidelity.
manualSteps: Read the cms_scope_expectation answer first: is HubSpot CMS being kept, moved, or moved as a separate programme?
Confirm separately whether any MARKETING EMAIL renders from a HubDB query — that half is in scope whatever happens to the website
If the content stays on HubSpot CMS, write the boundary into the scope document and stop
Inventory HubDB tables and every HubL query against them
Classify each query: static lookup / per-recipient dynamic / listing
Model each table as a Data Extension
Replace static lookups with AMPscript Lookup or a merge field
Pre-compute per-recipient dynamic values into the entry audience
Rebuild listing-style content as a dynamic block, or accept reduced fidelity
callouts.issue: CONDITIONAL ON SCOPE — where HubDB-backed content is expected to move, that content depends on tables queried at render time
callouts.gloss: HubDB is a relational store HubL queries WHILE RENDERING, and most of what it backs is HubSpot CMS — landing pages, site pages, blog listings. Whether any of that is in this migration is the cms_scope_expectation probe, not an assumption this callout gets to make. Where the answer is that it stays on HubSpot CMS, this is a boundary to write down and nothing more. Where the answer is that it moves, or where an EMAIL renders from a HubDB query, it is a blocker: nothing in Marketing Cloud renders from an arbitrary queried table at send time, so the data moves to a Data Extension and the render-time query becomes an AMPscript Lookup or a pre-computed value.

callouts.workaround: Classify every HubL construct before estimating, and estimate by construct count rather than by email count. Plain token becomes a merge field, mechanically. Conditional or loop over the contact's own attributes becomes a dynamic content block. A HubDB or CRM-object query needs the data pre-joined first. Macro, include and filter chains are rebuilt as a target-native block. Render-diff the top-volume emails against production samples rather than trusting the rewrite.
manualSteps: Pull template and module source via the CMS API and inventory HubL constructs
Classify each construct: token / attribute conditional / data query / macro chain
Rebuild in Content Builder, using AMPscript where the construct needs logic
Render-diff the output against production samples for the top-volume emails
callouts.issue: Email, template, or module contains HubL beyond simple token substitution
callouts.gloss: HubL is a full templating language. Plain tokens port to merge fields trivially; loops, conditionals, macros, filters, includes and HubDB or CRM queries do not. Against classic Marketing Cloud this is a rewrite into AMPscript, not a redesign.

callouts.workaround: Do not port module by module. Inventory modules by USAGE COUNT, build a small library of content blocks and templates covering the high-usage ones, and inline the long tail with a record of what was dropped. Budget the library build as its own task BEFORE content migration starts, and warn the client that the editor's workflow changes — that is a change-management item, not a build item.
manualSteps: Export module source and field definitions via the CMS API
Rank modules by usage count across emails and email templates; rank site usage separately and only if cms_scope_expectation says the web estate is moving
Design a Content Builder block and template library covering the top modules
Inline or retire the long tail, and record what was dropped
Brief the content team on the editing-experience change before cutover
callouts.issue: Content is assembled from custom modules — parameterised HubL components with typed fields
callouts.gloss: A mature HubSpot content system is a module library, not a set of emails. Content Builder has content blocks and template slots, which recover part of the reuse but not the typed-field component model, so the abstraction flattens unless a target-side library is built first.

callouts.workaround: Run the site form scan FIRST — it is the one HubSpot capability the accelerator already has, and it finds embeds on customer-owned domains that no tenant export will ever show you. Reconcile what it finds against the in-tenant form inventory; the delta is the real risk. Then disposition each embed: port to a CloudPage with Web Collect, bridge it (keep the HubSpot form posting and relay submissions), rebuild, or retire. Bridging is often the only way to avoid a big-bang website change.
manualSteps: Run a site form scan across all customer-owned domains before scoping forms
Reconcile discovered embeds against the in-tenant form inventory
Identify who owns each hosting web property and whether they have capacity
Disposition each form and CTA: port / bridge / rebuild / retire
Inventory legacy versus new-editor CTAs separately and state what happens to each one's analytics history
Plan the embed swap as a website release, on the web team's schedule, not marketing's
callouts.issue: HubSpot forms and CTAs are embedded across customer-owned web properties
callouts.gloss: Forms and CTAs are embed scripts served from HubSpot and dropped into pages marketing may not own. Target-side they become CloudPages plus Web Collect, and every swap is a website release on somebody else's schedule.

callouts.workaround: Transcribe rule-based scoring and rebuild it target-side, accepting that decay and time-frame criteria may need explicit date attributes. Migrate predictive values as a dated, frozen snapshot for continuity, declare an explicit end-of-life for that snapshot, and plan the replacement model as a post-migration workstream with its own budget. Warn Sales explicitly: score-driven routing degrading is a sales-visible failure.
manualSteps: Transcribe every scoring rule set before tenant access ends
Identify which downstream automation and routing depends on score thresholds
Decide where scoring will live — Automation Studio query, or upstream in the CRM
Rebuild rule-based scoring and reconcile against a sample cohort
Export current predictive values as a dated snapshot and agree its expiry
Name the owner of the replacement model, and brief Sales
callouts.issue: Estate uses HubSpot lead scoring; predictive scores in particular have no exportable model
callouts.gloss: Rule-based scoring is readable and can be transcribed. Predictive scoring is not exportable at all — only current values come out, and classic Marketing Cloud has no native scoring engine to receive either, so scoring lands in a query, an automation, or upstream in the CRM.

callouts.workaround: Decide explicitly whether Sequences are in or out, in Assess rather than Execute. If in, they route to the Sales Cloud workstream rather than being absorbed here. If out, get it written down, and confirm what happens to them at HubSpot decommissioning — that is a hard dependency on the CRM decision above.
manualSteps: Ask Sales — not Marketing — whether Sequences are in use and how heavily
Establish the licence and budget owner
Record an explicit in-scope / out-of-scope decision in the engagement scope document
If out of scope, confirm what happens at HubSpot decommissioning
callouts.issue: Estate uses HubSpot Sequences — a Sales Hub capability outside the marketing migration's scope and budget
callouts.gloss: Sequences are rep-sent 1:1 cadences from a connected mailbox, licensed under Sales Hub and owned by Sales. The Salesforce counterpart is Sales Engagement — a different product, a different budget line, usually a different buyer.

callouts.workaround: Treat reporting as a parallel workstream from day one rather than a migration deliverable. Inventory the reports actually VIEWED — usually far fewer than the number that exist — rebuild those, and get written acceptance that pre-cutover attribution history does not come along. Retain a read-only HubSpot seat past cutover if historic reporting must stay reachable.
manualSteps: Inventory dashboards and saved reports; identify which are genuinely viewed, and by whom
Screenshot and document definitions manually — there is no reliable export
Establish who signs off marketing reporting; in a HubSpot estate this is frequently outside marketing
Scope the target reporting build as its own workstream with its own budget
Get written acceptance that pre-cutover attribution history does not migrate
Retain a read-only HubSpot seat past cutover if historic reporting must remain accessible
callouts.issue: Saved reports, dashboards, and attribution reports have no export path and no target equivalent
callouts.gloss: HubSpot's report builder spans marketing AND CRM objects in one query surface because they are one database. There is no API for report definitions, and classic Marketing Cloud's native reporting is materially weaker — so this is the gap most likely to be found after go-live, by an executive whose dashboard is empty.

callouts.workaround: Scope a workshop-led assessment with an explicitly reduced fidelity claim, or fund the adapter build. Either way, set the expectation in the SOW rather than at the first status meeting. The site form scan is the one automated HubSpot capability that does exist and it should be run early, because it finds the things no tenant export shows.
manualSteps: Set expectations in the SOW: HubSpot assessment is workshop-led, not adapter-led
Provision a scoped private-app token early — scope approval is a lead-time item
Run the site form scan for off-tenant forms
Use UI exports plus ad-hoc API scripts for the object inventory
Re-verify every verification_required entry in the HubSpot manifest before it drives a client-facing number
callouts.issue: The accelerator has no HubSpot source adapter — automated extraction and IR generation are not available
callouts.gloss: The MVP source matrix is Eloqua and SFMC. A HubSpot-source engagement gets no automated inventory, no canonical IR generation and no adapter-driven disposition. This is a delivery-capability gap, not a platform gap, and it is why the source end of this readout is interview-only.

readiness.questionText: How much is actually running today, and across how many business units or instances?

options.label: 500+ active campaigns or programs, or six or more business units / separate instances
150-500 active campaigns or programs, or three to five business units
40-150 active campaigns or programs across one or two business units
Fewer than 40 active campaigns or programs in a single business unit

readiness.questionText: Do you have working API credentials for the platform you are leaving and the one you are moving to?

options.label: No API access to the source platform, and no clear owner who could get it
Someone could probably get source access eventually; target access has not been discussed
Source access exists or is one short approval away; target access is being provisioned
Working API credentials exist for both, with an owner who can hand them over this week

readiness.measures: Whether credentials/API access exist to actually scan the source and write to the target

readiness.questionText: How complex are the journeys, flows and automations that are live today?

options.label: Heavily branched journeys with custom scripting and real-time triggers — most would be rebuilt from scratch
A mix, including several long-running journeys whose logic nobody has documented
Mostly scheduled or simply-triggered flows, with a few complex exceptions
A small number of straightforward, mostly scheduled flows that map cleanly onto the target

readiness.measures: Whether flows/journeys survive the move or have to be rebuilt

readiness.questionText: How are your emails, landing pages and templates built?

options.label: Bespoke code throughout — scripting embedded in most assets, no template governance
A governed template set exists, but many one-off assets have drifted away from it
Most sends come from a maintained template library; scripting is limited to a handful of assets
A small governed template set with no meaningful custom scripting

readiness.measures: Template governance versus bespoke code and scripting depth

readiness.questionText: How well is your data model documented, and are audiences reused or rebuilt each time?

options.label: No current schema documentation; audiences are built per campaign and rarely reused
Partial documentation; some shared audiences, but plenty of per-campaign duplicates
The core schema is documented and most audiences come from a shared, reusable set
Documented schema with a named owner, and audiences defined once and reused across campaigns

readiness.measures: Schema documentation and audience reuse versus per-campaign silos

readiness.questionText: What else writes into the platform — external forms, integrations, third-party tools?

options.label: Many external systems and third-party forms post in, and nobody has a full list
Several known integrations plus some third-party forms; the list is roughly known
A handful of documented integrations; forms are mostly native to the platform
Effectively self-contained — native forms and one or two documented integrations

readiness.measures: External forms and integrations posting into the platform

readiness.questionText: How are consent, preferences and suppressions handled today?

options.label: A custom-built preference centre plus bespoke suppression logic nobody fully owns
A customised preference centre with several suppression rules, only partly documented
Light customisation on top of standard preference handling; suppression rules are documented
Standard out-of-the-box preference and suppression handling only

readiness.questionText: Who decides what moves, what is retired and what is rebuilt — and who validates it afterwards?

options.label: No named owner for those decisions, and nobody free to validate the result
An owner exists in principle but has little time; validation would fall to one already-busy person
A named owner per area, with some capacity set aside to review and test
A named decision owner and named validators, with time formally allocated to the migration

readiness.measures: Whether humans exist to make disposition decisions and to validate the result

complexity.questionText: Roughly how many journeys or automated programs are live, and how are they triggered?

options.label: Fewer than 20 active journeys, mostly scheduled
20-80 journeys, a mix of triggered and scheduled
80+ journeys, heavily API-triggered with complex branching

complexity.measures: Volume and trigger mix of live journeys

complexity.questionText: How large and how relational is the data model behind your sends?

options.label: Mostly flat send lists, fewer than 30 tables in total
Some relational structure, 30-100 tables, moderate SQL
A complex relational model, 100+ tables, heavy SQL automation

complexity.measures: Volume and relational depth of the data model

complexity.questionText: How much custom scripting sits inside your emails, pages and automations?

options.label: Minimal scripting, no server-side code, no custom hosted pages
Moderate scripting, with one to five server-side scripts or hosted pages
Extensive scripting, server-side code throughout, hosted pages in active use

complexity.measures: How much custom code is embedded in assets and pages

complexity.questionText: How is the account split across business units or child accounts?

options.label: A single business unit, or a simple parent-child pair
Two to five business units with some shared assets
Six or more business units, or complex cross-unit content sharing

complexity.measures: How many business units and how much they share

complexity.questionText: How much of the platform is wired into other systems?

options.label: Basic native CRM sync only
Native sync plus a few API integrations
Custom REST/SOAP integrations across multiple external systems

complexity.measures: Breadth of external systems wired into the platform

complexity.questionText: How custom is the consent and suppression handling?

options.label: Standard publication or subscription lists only
Some custom suppression logic on top of the standard model
A custom preference centre with complex suppression rules

complexity.measures: Depth of custom preference and suppression logic
